attribution.note: Zitron's own summary line in his newsletter, stated as his conclusion.

semantics.note: Keeps 'entire', 'in the hands of', the gigawatt figure, the 'doesn't appear' qualifier and the crypto-revenue clause. A compound present-tense observation.

contract.note: Reading 'money' as revenue, using FY2024, and reading 'entire' as all planned buildout are ordinary readings. Treating 'doesn't appear' as asking whether public evidence of a prior AI facility existed is fair.

evidence.note: Audited FY2024 10-K, filed before the post, says self-mining is the majority of revenue. This supports the revenue clause.
Aug 2024 announcement of a 120 MW build for CoreWeave by Chirisa/PowerHouse with Blue Owl. A buildout with another developer defeats 'entire'.

Public 2019 announcement of a newly commissioned Core Scientific facility hosting DGX deep-learning gear. It undercuts 'doesn't appear' to have built one, though conversion versus new build is unclear.

reviews.rationale: The majority-crypto-revenue clause holds under the FY2024 filing (e1). The 'entire buildout' clause is contradicted by a separate CoreWeave development with Chirisa/PowerHouse announced in 2024 (e2). The no-apparent-AI-facility clause is undercut by Core Scientific's public 2019 DGX-ready datacenter announcement (e3). Only the revenue part holds.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his essay.

semantics.note: Faithful paraphrase. The capability clause is a rhetorical judgment with no testable standard. Only the spending clause is checkable in principle.

contract.note: The $200B minimum and the realized-spend reading are ordinary. The roster, start date and attribution to generative AI are evaluator choices. The contract correctly declines to invent a capability standard.

evidence.note: Alphabet's Q4 2024 release: a company claim about engagement from AI features. It gives no cumulative generative-AI spending and does not test the capability clause.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no cumulative generative-AI spending figure across the largest tech companies, so the 'hundreds of billions' clause is neither confirmed nor refuted. The capability clause has no identifiable standard and cannot be scored. The only item is a company disclosure that serves as context.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words, in a sidebar on benchmark gaming.

semantics.note: The source is a general maxim about honor systems under incentives. He explicitly says there is no accusation of cheating, only a possibility. The normalisation turns this into a claim that benchmark integrity often fails, and it drops that disclaimer.

contract.note: The support condition requires documented recurrent integrity failures, but the speaker disclaimed any accusation. 'Often' and 'real consequences' have no standard, so the contract supplies a testable reading the speaker did not give.

evidence.note: ABC piece on benchmark gaming risk. It records no cheating frequency or enforcement.
2024 LiveBench preprint showing independent, contamination-resistant evaluation exists. It does not measure cheating or sanctions.
2015 ImageNet sanction on Baidu. It is a different benchmark and period, but shows that some consequences have existed.

reviews.rationale: The sentence is a general warning that honor systems tend to fail under large incentives, offered while expressly disclaiming any accusation of cheating. It has no frequency threshold, scope or consequence standard that could be checked. The evidence is all context and could not settle it anyway.

attribution.note: Zitron's own analytical conclusion ('based on my analysis').

semantics.note: Keeps the $40B+ figure, the 'does not appear' qualifier and both alternatives (more debt or selling stakes). The 'AI' label on the commitments matches the context (OpenAI, Stargate).

contract.note: Judging liquidity against the commitments' payment needs at the latest balance-sheet date is a reasonable reading. Whether 'have the money' means cash on hand or funding over the schedule is an evaluator choice that decides the result.

evidence.note: SoftBank's Dec 2024 disclosure implies about $20.8B stand-alone and $34.1B consolidated liquidity, both below $40B. It gives no payment schedule or future receipts, so funding need is not shown.
April 2025 terms, after the post: SoftBank's effective share is up to $30B after syndication, with staged closings. Later financing choices are context only under the contract.

reviews.rationale: Reported liquidity was below the stated commitments, which is consistent with the claim. But the packet has no reconciled payment schedule, future cash receipts or alternative non-debt funding, which the contract requires to show a material financing gap. The later terms are context only. The evidence does not settle it.
